ap_physics_1-f01.title: Atwood machine

stimulus.description: Two blocks of masses $m_1=1.5\text{ kg}$ and $m_2=2\text{ kg}$ hang from the two ends of a light string that passes over a light, frictionless pulley (an Atwood machine). The blocks are released from rest with block 2 at a height $h=1\text{ m}$ above the floor.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents block 2 (the heavier block), draw and label the forces (not components) that act on it while the blocks move. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Two arrows from the dot: weight straight down and tension straight up. The weight arrow is longer than the tension arrow because block 2 accelerates downward.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels the two forces: weight (down) and tension (up), with no extra force such as a force of motion
common_errors: adds a force of motion downward

rubric_rows.criterion: Arrow directions are correct: weight straight down and tension straight up
common_errors: draws tension down

rubric_rows.criterion: The weight arrow is longer than the tension arrow, consistent with a downward acceleration
common_errors: draws the two arrows with equal length

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks in terms of $m_1$, $m_2$, and fundamental constants.
parts.model_answer: $m_2g-T=m_2a$ and $T-m_1g=m_1a$, so $a=\dfrac{(m_2-m_1)g}{m_1+m_2}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Newton's second law to block 2: $m_2g-T=m_2a$
common_errors: uses T = m2 g

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Newton's second law to block 1: $T-m_1g=m_1a$
common_errors: uses a different tension for the second block
gets the sign of the acceleration wrong

rubric_rows.criterion: Combines the equations to the correct expression $a=(m_2-m_1)g/(m_1+m_2)$
common_errors: adds the masses in the numerator

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of block 2 just before it reaches the floor for $m_1=1.5\text{ kg}$, $m_2=2\text{ kg}$ and $h=1\text{ m}$.
parts.model_answer: $a=1.40\text{ m/s}^2$ and $v=\sqrt{2ah}=\sqrt{2(1.40)(1)}\approx 1.67\text{ m/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the acceleration (about 1.40) from the expression in part B
common_errors: uses the sum of the masses in the numerator

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses $v^2=2ah$ to find a speed of about 1.67 with units of meters per second
common_errors: forgets the square root

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The masses of both blocks are doubled, so that they are $2m_1$ and $2m_2$. Does the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks increase, decrease, or stay the same? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The acceleration stays the same. In $a=(m_2-m_1)g/(m_1+m_2)$ the factor of 2 appears in the numerator and in the denominator and cancels.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the acceleration stays the same
common_errors: states that the acceleration doubles

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that doubling both masses doubles the net force and doubles the total mass, so the acceleration does not change
common_errors: argues only that heavier objects fall at the same rate

ap_physics_1-f02.title: Elevator motion in three stages: v-t graph and scale reading

stimulus.description: A person of mass $m=60\text{ kg}$ stands on a scale in an elevator that moves upward along a vertical shaft. Starting from rest, the elevator speeds up uniformly with acceleration $a_1=1\text{ m/s}^2$ for $t_1=2\text{ s}$, then moves at constant velocity for $t_2=4\text{ s}$, and then slows down uniformly to a stop in $t_3=2\text{ s}$. The scale reads the magnitude of the normal force on the person. Blank axes for the graphs are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the velocity $v$ of the elevator as a function of time $t$ for the whole trip. Label the axes with quantities and units and label the key values of velocity and time.
parts.model_answer: A straight line from the origin up to $v=2.00\text{ m/s}$ at $t=2\text{ s}$, a horizontal line at that velocity until $t=6\text{ s}$, and a straight line down to zero at $t=8\text{ s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Both axes are labeled with quantities and units and a scale is shown
common_errors: omits units

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a straight line from the origin rising to about $2.00\text{ m/s}$ at $t=2\text{ s}$
common_errors: draws a curve instead of a straight line for uniform acceleration

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a horizontal segment at the same velocity from $t=2\text{ s}$ to $t=6\text{ s}$
common_errors: draws the constant-velocity segment with a slope

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a straight line down to zero velocity at $t=8\text{ s}$
common_errors: ends the graph below zero velocity

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Determine the total distance that the elevator rises during the whole trip. Show how you use your graph from part A.
parts.model_answer: The displacement is the area under the $v$–$t$ graph: $y=\tfrac12(2.00)(2)+(2.00)(4)+\tfrac12(2.00)(2)\approx 12.0\text{ m}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the displacement as the area under the velocity-time graph
required_elements: displacement is the area under the v-t graph
common_errors: uses the slope of the graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Adds the areas of the triangle, the rectangle, and the second triangle: $\tfrac12vt_1+vt_2+\tfrac12vt_3$
common_errors: omits one of the three areas

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates a total distance of about 12.0 with units of meters
common_errors: uses the average velocity of only the first segment

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the reading of the scale (the magnitude of the normal force on the person) during the first stage, when the elevator is speeding up. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: Newton's second law gives $N-mg=ma_1$, so $N=m(g+a_1)=(60)(9.8+1)\approx 648\text{ N}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Newton's second law to the person with the normal force up and the weight down: $N-mg=ma_1$
common_errors: uses N = m g
subtracts the acceleration term

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for the normal force: $N=m(g+a_1)$
common_errors: gets $N=m(g-a_1)$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates a reading of about 648 with units of newtons
common_errors: uses a mass in the units of newtons

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: In a second trip the constant-velocity stage is made $3\text{ s}$ longer while everything else is unchanged. By how much does the total distance that the elevator rises change, and does the reading of the scale during the constant-velocity stage change? Justify your answers.
parts.model_answer: The distance increases by $v\Delta t=2.00\times3=6.0\text{ m}$ (an added rectangle under the graph). The reading does not change, because during constant velocity the acceleration is zero so $N=mg=588\text{ N}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the distance increases by about 6.0 with units of meters and the scale reading does not change
common_errors: states that the distance does not change
states that the reading changes

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with the added rectangle of height equal to the constant velocity and with zero acceleration so that the normal force equals the weight
common_errors: argues only that the elevator travels longer

ap_physics_1-f03.title: Experiment: gravitational field strength from a cart on an incline

stimulus.description: A student releases a low-friction cart from rest on a track that is tilted at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, and measures the acceleration of the cart down the track with a motion sensor. The student repeats the experiment for several angles and wants to determine the gravitational field strength $g$.

notes: A student releases a low-friction cart from rest on a track that is tilted at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, and measures the acceleration of the cart down the track with a motion sensor. parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the acceleration as a function of the angle. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the independent variable is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the measured angle.
parts.model_answer: Use a protractor (or measure the height of the raised end and the length of the track and find the angle from a trigonometric ratio) to set each angle of the track and a motion sensor to measure the acceleration; change only the angle with the same cart and track; reduce the uncertainty in the angle by measuring the height and the length with a meterstick and calculating the angle.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies a way to set and measure the angle and a way to measure the acceleration (motion sensor or a time and distance measurement)
required_elements: a way to measure the angle and a way to measure the acceleration

rubric_rows.criterion: Changes only the angle while using the same cart and the same track (both conditions are needed)
required_elements: change only the angle with the same cart and track

rubric_rows.criterion: Reduces the uncertainty in the angle by calculating it from the height and the length measured with a meterstick, or by repeating the measurement and averaging (either earns the point)
required_elements: calculate the angle from the height and the length or repeat and average (either earns the point)

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies $a$ (vertical) versus $\sin\theta$ (horizontal)
common_errors: plots a versus theta

parts.prompt: On a blank grid whose scale you choose, plot the data in a form that gives a straight line, and draw a best-fit line. Label the axes with quantities and units and use a scale that fills most of the grid.

common_errors: scale uses less than half the grid

common_errors: uses slope = 1/g
